newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia says it will not postpone November 18 polls.
newsitem.headline: Zambia says it will not postpone November 18 polls.

text.p: The Zambian government said on Wednesday it would not postpone general elections scheduled for November 18 despite a boycott of the polls by seven opposition parties.
Vice-President Godfrey Miyanda said the government saw no reason to postpone the elections, adding that in any case only the Electoral Commission could defer the polls.
"Our position is that we are not aware of any plausible reasons why the elections should be postponed," Miyanda told a news conference.
"There is no justification for the elections to be put off, but we leave this to the appropriate body to handle in accordance with our laws," he said.

Electoral Commission chairman Judge Bobby Bwalya told Reuters: "There is no provision for the postponement of the elections. Once the date has been set and nominations have been filed, the process is irreversible."

Seven opposition parties, including former president Kenneth Kaunda's United National Independence Party (UNIP), are boycotting the elections which they say have been arranged to ensure that President Frederick Chiluba's Movement for Multi-party Democracy (MMD) remains in office.
The parties oppose a new constitution barring some candidates, including Kaunda, from standing for president if they are first-generation Zambians.
Kaunda, whose parents were Malawian, ruled after independence from Britain in 1964 until 1991 when he lost to Chiluba in Zambia's first multi-party elections in 17 years.
Chiluba has been under local and international pressure to postpone the polls and allow the former president -- who leads the largest opposition party -- to stand for election.
But Miyanda said on Wednesday the government did not intend to reverse changes to the electoral process to allow Kaunda's UNIP to contest the polls.
"Those who make irresponsible and hasty decisions have to answer to their members," he told reporters.
Lusaka's Supreme Court has delayed a ruling on a last-minute petition filed by the opposition parties challenging Chiluba's eligibility to stand.
Chiluba's origins have been a source of much speculation in Zambia. Some newspapers and opposition parties say that he was born in Zaire.
The court's decision is expected on Thursday.
